newsitem.title: SUDAN: Carter sees Sudanese leader on peace in south.
newsitem.headline: Carter sees Sudanese leader on peace in south.

text.p: Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter met Sudanese President Omar Hassan al-Bashir in Khartoum on Sunday and state television said they discussed bringing more southern groups into a peace agreement with Khartoum.

Carter has been trying to bring together the Sudanese government and the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA), which has been fighting in the south since 1983 and which has refused to sign the peace agreement.

The television quoted Carter as saying his meeting with Bashir "dealt with the peace process and the possibilities of expansion to include other groups, besides examining the issue of peace between Sudan and its neighbours".

The government will sign the peace agreement with small former rebel groups on Monday at a ceremony to be attended by foreign dignitaries including Central African Republic President Ange-Felix Patasse, OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmad Salim and Chadian Interior Minister Nimir Ahmat.
It was not clear if Jimmy Carter would attend the signing.

The government newspaper al-Sudan al-Hadith said the agreement provides for a general amnesty. The factions which sign will retain command of their forces for a four-year transitional period, under the supervision of the armed forces.
These forces have already turned into pro-government militias in the south, harassing the SPLA on Khartoum's behalf.

Independent analysts say the peace agreement shows that Khartoum can find allies in the south but that they doubt it will make much difference on the ground, where the mainstream SPLA has made significant advances this year.
The SPLA has rejected the peace agreement as a sham. In alliance with northern opposition groups, it is fighting to overthrow the Islamist government.
